source.title: How Effective Can Dropout Be in Multiple Instance Learning ?
source.authors: Wen-Hui Zhu; Pei-Jie Qiu; Xi-Wen Chen; Zhangsihao Yang; Aristeidis Sotiras; Abolfazl Razi; Yalin Wang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices and rebuttal experiments.
record.tranche_reason: Tests dropout’s effect on held-out performance in multiple instance learning, a new setting for the dropout generalization claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for instance dropout and its proposed MIL-Dropout. It also discusses cited prior work on dropout, which is not recorded as this study’s result.
record.test_reason: The standard neuron-dropout experiments bear on V6 in a new setting: fully connected feature extractors in MIL classifiers. Instance masking and the proposed MIL-Dropout are different interventions and do not directly test the dropout claim as specified.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: dropping selected instances can improve MIL performance and generalization, and MIL-Dropout systematically selects those instances. They also report degradation and convergence failure with aggressive masking and Transformer-block integration. Their conclusion concerns dropout-like instance masking; the principal baseline comparisons do not isolate its contribution from added feature-extractor layers.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests instance-level dropout in weakly supervised MIL and proposes a method that drops highly attended and similar instances. It does not test the original paper’s standard dropout setup in ordinary fully connected or convolutional classifiers.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset-dependent optimal K; excessive dropout degrades performance, and integration into Transformer blocks fails to converge.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed MIL-Dropout configurations improve benchmark and WSI classification performance, but the main comparisons also add trainable feature-extractor layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding an instance-masking feature-extractor package can improve MIL classification performance relative to the reported original-model baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: Aggressive instance masking reduces ABMIL accuracy, and instance masking inside Transformer blocks fails to converge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MIL instance masking depends on the number of masked instances and its placement in the architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout1 configurations reduce accuracy, but the intervention is undefined.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An intervention identified as Dropout1 harms ABMIL performance at the reported settings; its relation to neuron or instance dropout cannot be determined.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 3 associates flatter loss landscapes with better noise-corrupted test AUC.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these MIL experiments, unscaled curvature-based sharpness accompanies robustness to input corruption.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025).
record.problems: The central experiments concern weakly supervised MIL with pretrained tile embeddings, not the ordinary fully connected and convolutional classifiers named in V6. Some ablation results are figure-only, and the reported WSI averages do not include uncertainty in the cited passage.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2’s separate per-aggregator accuracy, F1, and AUC results are not extracted; Section 6.2’s aggregate improvements are retained instead. Figure 3 noise-attack comparisons and Figure 4 strategy comparisons are figure-only, and their values are not included. Appendix C Table 7 survival-prediction results are outside V6’s classification claim.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance performance under random labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.

Controlled training-set-size comparisons; ordinary end-to-end convolutional classifiers; joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation. Reported high-rate convergence failures do not quantify training underfitting.
Magnitude-scaled perturbations, training–test error gaps at similarly low training loss, and rankings against norm/margin measures.
Removal of examples selected by memorization influence versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: The stated performance improvements from standard dropout with p=0.1 are not recorded. Extract a qualitative row and preserve the absence of dataset-specific values and uncertainty.

record.verdict_notes: Instance masking is not example removal followed by retraining and therefore does not test V8. The sharpness analysis lacks V7's magnitude scaling and generalization-gap comparison. Figure-only results and Table 2 details were already declared omitted, so they are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Small training-set behavior, conventional dropout in fully connected and convolutional classifiers outside MIL, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ABMIL
rows.operation_detail: Added standard dropout with p=0.4.
rows.note: The paper groups these as aggressive dropout results and states that dropping a large proportion of instances degrades performance.
rows.check: Accuracy falls from 86.3% to 66.2%. This is an excessive-dropout condition explicitly described as failing to converge; it supports V6's excessive-dropout qualification rather than challenging suitably configured dropout.

relationships.condition: Standard dropout at aggressive rates in ABMIL on CAMELYON16
relationships.reason: R17–R18 show accuracy falling from 86.3% to 66.2% and 53.4%, consistent with V6's qualification that excessive dropout harms learning; the text reports convergence failure.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy fell from 86.3% to 66.2% in one comparison and to 53.4% in another. Convergence failure was reported without direct evidence of underfitting from training error.
